newsitem.title: USA: California localities join suit against BankAmerica.
newsitem.headline: California localities join suit against BankAmerica.

text.p: Nine local governments in California are joining San Francisco in suing BankAmerica Corp., the nation's third largest bank, for allegedly mismanaging municipal bond funds, attorneys said on Tuesday.
The localities have joined lawsuits filed in May by the city and county of San Francisco, and by California Attorney General Dan Lungren, San Francisco Deputy City Attorney Matt Davis told Reuters.

The San Francisco and state lawsuits, filed in San Francisco Superior Court, alleged that BankAmerica unit Bank of America overcharged bond issuers, failed to return unclaimed funds from bond trust accounts, and improperly invested funds from some of the accounts.
BankAmerica spokesman John Keane said the bank has yet to be served with the additional complaints, but added: "As we understand, there is no new information here."
"Our response to the basic issues is the same. We believe that we have refunded any overcharges but are ready to make good on any others that can be substantiated," Keane said.
He added that Bank of America believes the investments it made were appropriate, and that it has fully returned unclaimed funds from the bond accounts.

Davis said the California counties of Riverside, Marin, Contra Costa, Santa Clara, Sonoma, Solano and Tulare were joining the lawsuit, along with the city of Industry and the Industry Urban Development Agency. They will be represented by the San Francisco city attorney's office.
Davis said several other local governments were likely to join the case before the end of the month. "I think a lot will (join) before the dust settles," he said.
The lawsuits were based on a so-called "whistleblower" complaint filed under seal in April 1995 by Patrick Stull, a former vice president for corporate trust at Bank of America.
San Francisco sued for more than $12 million, alleging that the bank, acting as a trustee, mishandled bond funds issued for low-income housing, schools, fire protection and other public works.
Lungren's lawsuit said more than $100 billion of bond funds were placed in state and local government accounts administered by the bank between 1978 and 1993.
"The bank lost money in those accounts through errors, mistakes, theft and poor management," the lawsuit alleged.
Lungren alleged that state and local governments suffered "hundreds of millions of dollars" in damages.
Keane said Bank of America discovered the overcharges on its own and voluntarily made refunds.
"Our objective here is to do what is right," Keane said. "However, there is a significant difference between what we believe Bank of America owed and what the suits are claiming."
